title: Solipsism: This Is All In My Mind?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore solipsism, the philosophical view that only one's own mind is certain to exist. They trace its roots to ancient skepticism and Zhuangzi's dream argument, Descartes' methodic doubt and "I think therefore I am," and the term's 19th-century coinage. They cover varieties of solipsism (metaphysical, epistemological, methodological, ethical), modern versions like the brain-in-a-vat, the simulation hypothesis, and Nozick's experience machine, and critiques including Samuel Johnson's rock kick, Wittgenstein, Stephen P. Thornton, and Bertrand Russell's glitch argument. They also discuss philosophical zombies, derealization in schizophrenia, and a listener email from Jun inviting the show to Germany.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to solipsism
segments.summary: Hosts introduce solipsism as the idea that only one's own mind exists, calling it annoying but a useful argument for testing philosophers.

segments.title: Ancient skeptics and dreams
segments.summary: The skeptics of the third century BCE argued knowledge is not certain because senses can be deceived, including by dreams. Solipsism is described as an extreme form of skepticism, sometimes called global skepticism.

segments.title: Zhuangzi and Descartes
segments.summary: Zhuangzi's dream about being a butterfly raised doubts about waking reality. Descartes in the seventeenth century introduced methodic doubt and the evil demon idea, leading to 'I think therefore I am'.

segments.title: Other minds and the origin of the term solipsism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the problem of other minds: we cannot prove others have experiences. They note the word came from Latin roots meaning alone and self, appearing in 1869, and that no great philosopher endorsed it.

segments.title: Other minds, color experience, and philosophical zombies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss inverted color experience, brain-to-brain connection thought experiments, and philosophical zombies that act human but lack experience. They relate this to AI consciousness.

segments.title: Varieties of solipsism
segments.summary: Metaphysical, epistemological, methodological, and ethical solipsism are defined. Casper Hare's book On Myself and Other Less Important Subjects is cited for a version of ethical solipsism, and the hosts criticize it as a bad idea.

segments.title: Brain in a vat, simulation hypothesis
segments.summary: The brain-in-a-vat and matrix scenarios are described, and the simulation hypothesis from Nick Bostrom is distinguished from the brain-in-a-vat idea, with a comparison to creationism.

segments.title: Nozick's experience machine
segments.summary: Robert Nozick's 1974 thought experiment asks whether people would plug into a machine providing simulated pleasant experiences. Most people decline, which the hosts use against pure hedonism.

segments.title: Samuel Johnson's rock and Wittgenstein
segments.summary: Samuel Johnson reportedly refuted Berkeley's idealism by kicking a rock. Wittgenstein is discussed as holding that some things must be taken as given to avoid spinning wheels. Pronunciation of his name is debated.

segments.title: Stephen P. Thornton and Bertrand Russell
segments.summary: Stephen P. Thornton argues that mental states are learned through an intersubjective world, which refutes solipsism. Bertrand Russell argued that waking life lacks the randomness of dreams, which leads to the Glitch in the Matrix idea.

segments.title: Derealization, schizophrenia, and ethical solipsism disorders
segments.summary: Derealization is described as a frightening experience in paranoid schizophrenia where others seem unreal. Clara S. Humpston is cited on retreat into solipsistic states for control. Narcissistic and antisocial personality traits are linked to ethical solipsism.

segments.title: Listener mail from Jun about a German tour
segments.summary: A listener named Jun, who works in wastewater R&D and wrote a PhD on waterless toilets, praised the show and invited the hosts to Germany, saying a 500-seat hall would sell out. The hosts respond positively.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and give the email address for contact.
